summary: Specifies a framework for SIP session policies. It gives proxy servers, which define and influence policies on call routing and other call features, a standard way to define or influence the policies of a session. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Proxies in phone calls act like receptionists who may set house rules. This memo gives a standard way for them to tell callers what the rules are.

questions: what is a sip policy server
session specific vs session independent policies
subtitle: How SIP proxies and network policy servers can tell phones and other endpoints the rules for a session before they break them.

tldr.problem: Networks often enforce rules on sessions, such as no video or a bandwidth cap, but enforcement usually silently blocks traffic and leaves the user confused.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines session-independent policies, fetched by subscription when a device starts, and session-specific policies, where a proxy points the device to a policy server that the device then contacts over a separate policy channel.
tldr.outcome: A user agent learns the rules, applies them to its session descriptions, and the provider can still enforce them. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6794 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its policy channel is defined in RFC 6795 and its policy data format in RFC 6796.

sections.title: Why Sessions Need Policies
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) sets up multimedia sessions such as audio, video and session-mode messaging. Proxy servers route requests and handle rendezvous, authentication and mobility, but they are divorced from the sessions themselves. The details of a session travel in message bodies, usually described with the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

The RFC gives two examples of why intermediaries want a say. A wireless network with scarce resources may want to restrict the bandwidth of each user, and a provider may have a service level agreement that limits the media types a user can use. In another case a firewall or network border device needs media sent to a specific IP address and port. Without signaling, enforcement mechanisms just drop packets and the user sees a device that malfunctions for no visible reason.

Session policies pair consent with enforcement: the user becomes aware of the policy and has to act on it, while the provider keeps the right to enforce it. Using the policy mechanism also avoids inspecting or modifying SIP message bodies.
sections.eli5: If a school quietly blocks a website, you just see a broken page. It is much better if the school posts the rules so you know what is allowed.

sections.title: Session-Independent Policies
sections.content:
Session-independent policies are created without reference to any one session and generally apply to everything a user agent sets up. They tend to stay stable for a while but can change, for example a lower bandwidth limit in peak hours and a higher one off-peak. The policy server tells the user agent when they change.

A user agent may get them from one or more policy servers, typically one in the local network domain and possibly one in the SIP service provider domain. The steps are: discover the servers, request the policies (typically at start up or when joining a new network), let the server pick the policies for this user, and let the server update them later.

A compliant user agent MUST support retrieval through the ua-profile event package of RFC 6080, using the local-network profile type for the local policy server and the user profile type for the provider. It MUST support the media policy data set of RFC 6796 and signals this by listing application/media-policy-dataset+xml in the Accept header field of its SUBSCRIBE.

The user agent MUST apply the policies it receives. If it decides not to use them, it MUST NOT set up a session unless it changes the domain that provided them. If it fails to subscribe it SHOULD NOT retry, except with a longer interval such as once every 24 hours. When both kinds of policy exist, session-independent policies are applied to the session description before it goes to the session-specific policy server.
sections.eli5: These are the standing house rules you get when you walk in the door, like no running. They apply to everything you do, and you are told if they change.

sections.title: Session-Specific Policies and Their Players
sections.content:
Session-specific policies are created for one particular session and can change during it. For example, a user can run out of credit mid-session, and the network then disallows all media from that point on.

The entities are a user agent, a proxy, a policy server and possibly a policy enforcement entity. The proxy is only a rendezvous point: it makes sure the user agent has the URI of the policy server in its domain, but it does not deliver the policies. The policy server receives session information from the user agent, decides which policies apply and returns them. How it makes decisions is out of scope. The RFC makes no assumptions about enforcement and calls the mechanism orthogonal to it.

Each domain on the signaling path may run its own policy server and a proxy that can introduce it, though the RFC expects session-specific policies will often come only from the user agent's local domain.
sections.eli5: The front desk (the proxy) only tells you which office to visit. The office (the policy server) is the one that actually tells you what is allowed for your visit today.

sections.title: The Separate Policy Channel
sections.content:
SIP signaling is used only to bring the user agent and the policy server together. After that they talk directly over a separate policy channel, rather than piggybacking policy data on SIP messages. The RFC lists the benefits: signaling and policy exchange can use different encryption, policies do not travel along a signaling path that may cross many domains, endpoints disclose only what each server asks for, and a server can push an update at any time. The disadvantage is extra messages.

On the channel the user agent submits information about the session and asks if it is permissible. The server answers with one of three decisions: deny the session, propose changes that would make it acceptable, or accept it as proposed. Later it can update that decision, for instance changing the available bandwidth or denying a session that was already accepted.

In the first worked example the offer is in the INVITE. Proxy A rejects the first INVITE with a 488 (Not Acceptable Here) carrying the policy server URI. The user agent discloses its offer, gets policies, and resends the INVITE with a Policy-ID header field. The called side gets a Policy-Contact header field from its own proxy and does the same, and the caller later contacts its server again with the offer and answer. When the offer is in the response, the caller contacts its policy server before sending the answer in the ACK, which needs that server to respond immediately.
sections.eli5: You get sent to the right office once. After that you and the office talk directly, so the front desk does not have to carry messages back and forth.

sections.title: Rendezvous and the New Header Fields
sections.content:
A user agent that supports the extension MUST put the option tag policy in a Supported header field of every request that can start an offer/answer exchange (INVITE, UPDATE, PRACK), even one with no offer. A proxy that sees this tag MAY reject the request with a 488 and a Policy-Contact header field holding one or more policy server URIs. It MUST first check that the request does not already carry a Policy-ID with its own policy server URI. A proxy can also add Policy-Contact to a forwarded request to point the called side to a server, appending to the end of the list so the order is kept.

The user agent decides whether to continue. If it does, it contacts the server, applies the policies and resends the request with a Policy-ID header field naming each server it contacted, plus an opaque token if the server supplied one. The token can help a domain route all requests of one session to the same proxy and policy server, for example when that server has configured a session border device. Tokens MUST NOT be cached, because a token is valid for one request only.

Several URIs with different schemes can be listed as alternatives for the same policy by giving them an identical alt-uri parameter. The user agent contacts one of each group, and a SIP or SIPS URI MUST always be included. The parameter non-cacheable stops a user agent from caching the URI. Otherwise a user agent SHOULD cache the URI of its local policy server, and the default maximum cached validity is 24 hours.

The called side MUST contact all listed servers in order, or reject with a 488 if it does not accept the policies. It MAY go ahead if a server is unreachable, so that a failed server does not stop communication.
sections.eli5: The proxy hands you a note with the office address. When you come back you show a stamp from the office so the front desk knows you already went.

sections.title: Managing the Policy Channel
sections.content:
A user agent MUST set up a policy channel to every discovered policy server. If it does not want to, it MUST cancel or reject the pending INVITE, or end the session if it is already running. It MUST keep each channel for the life of the session unless the server closes it or stops being relevant, and it MUST tell the server when the session ends so resources can be freed, unless the server said that is unnecessary.

For SIP and SIPS policy server URIs the user agent MUST use the event package of RFC 6795 as the channel. Other channel mechanisms are allowed. The user agent MUST support the media policy data set of RFC 6796 as the policy format.

A user agent MUST contact all of its servers before sending or after receiving a mid-dialog request, in the order discovered. It usually contacts a server twice in an offer/answer exchange. When one server returns information that others need, for example two media intermediaries that must know each other's address and port, the called side MUST contact all servers a second time. If a mid-dialog request gets a 488 with a new policy server, the caller retries as if it were the first request in the dialog to rediscover the list.

Policies MUST be applied to the offer and to the answer. If they are unacceptable, the user agent MUST NOT continue. When a policy update arrives, it MUST apply it or end the session. If the session description changes, for example because video is no longer allowed, it renegotiates with a re-INVITE or UPDATE.
sections.eli5: Once you know the offices, you must check in with each of them and tell them when you leave. If an office changes the rules mid-visit, you change what you are doing or you leave.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Policy enforcement without signaling can create a denial of service, since users cannot tell why sessions fail. Signaling the policies helps sessions pass enforcement. On the other hand, policies can change a user agent's behavior and an attacker could use them to cripple it, for example by setting the available bandwidth to zero during a session so it ends.

Session information can be sensitive, and so can policies, which may reveal network details or service level agreements. The RFC names four things to protect: the integrity of the policy server URI, authentication of the server and if needed the user agent, confidentiality of the exchange, and not sending private information even over a protected session.

A user agent SHOULD use TLS between itself and its proxies, because an attacker could remove the policy header fields or swap in the URI of a compromised server. It is RECOMMENDED that the user agent authenticate policy servers and that administrators use SIPS URIs. A user agent should accept session-independent policies only from trustworthy servers, since they affect every session. Policy servers SHOULD authenticate user agents but MAY give a generic policy to those they cannot authenticate.
sections.eli5: Make sure the note with the office address is real and not swapped by a prankster, and do not tell the office your secrets just to get an answer.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers two SIP header fields, Policy-ID and Policy-Contact, neither with a short form. It registers the non-cacheable parameter for Policy-Contact in the Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values registry. It also adds the SIP option tag policy, which indicates that a user agent can process policy server URIs and subscribe to session-specific policies.
sections.eli5: It adds the new names to the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE TWO NEW HEADER FIELDS (RFC 6794, SECTION 4.4.5)

data.title: Policy-ID and Policy-Contact
data.code:
Policy-ID        = "Policy-ID" HCOLON policyURI
                   *(COMMA  policyURI)
policyURI        = ( SIP-URI / SIPS-URI / absoluteURI )
                   [ SEMI token-param ] *( SEMI generic-param )
token-param      = "token=" token

Policy-Contact         = "Policy-Contact" HCOLON policyContact-info
                         *(COMMA policyContact-info)
policyContact-info     = LAQUOT policyContact-uri RAQUOT
                         *( SEMI policyContact-param )
policyContact-uri      = ( SIP-URI / SIPS-URI / absoluteURI )
policyContact-param    = ( "non-cacheable" / policyContact-alt-uri
                         / generic-param )
policyContact-alt-uri  = "alt-uri" EQUAL hostname
